speaker: randwallis
text: Good morning and welcome to an oral argument session of the Fifth District Court of Appeal. My name is Rand Wallace. I will be presiding over the OAs today. We have two other judges on the panel. First from our court, Meredith Sasso from Orange County. And we also have the privilege of having Judge Michael Orfinger here from the Seventh Circuit. He's helping us out here today with the cases. Wanna thank Judge Orfinger for taking time out of his busy schedule here to help us out. And we've got one case set for 9 a.m. That is Rashan Sagar versus the state of Florida. I'm going to assume that the plaintiff, Mr. McClain, that you would like five minutes of rebuttal unless you tell me differently. And then I would just ask everybody, if you're not speaking, that you would try and keep your mic on mute. Obviously on mute when you wanna ask a question or speak, but that way we can keep any kind of background noise to a minimum. So other than that, Mr. McClain, you are welcome to proceed.

speaker: matthewmclain
text: Good morning, Your Honors. Matt McClain on behalf of the appellant, Rashan Sagar. I would like to reserve five minutes for rebuttal as Judge Wallace previously noted. This is a juvenile offender resentencing case. Mr. Sagar was 16 at the time of the offense. He went ahead, entered a plea, negotiated originally to 30 years. Based off developments in juvenile resentencing law, eventually he filed for post-conviction relief, asking for relief from his sentence. Based off stipulation, the parties agreed to a 15 year sentence review. The court held the sentence review hearing. Both parties entered evidence in the case. The court then took the matter under advisement without issuing a decision at that moment. In its order, it goes through the different factors laid out by section 921.1402. Honestly, the factors weigh for and against Mr. Sagar. There are several factors such as his age, his sincere, sustained remorse, his participation in programs, many things that weigh against him. There are some things that weigh for him, excuse me, regarding things that weighed against him were the victim's family's feelings towards him, that he wasn't an active participant in the crime. But ultimately the court's decision came down to immigration consequences. And that was brought up during the evidentiary portion of the case that-

speaker: randwallis
text: Mr. McClain, the immigration issue was initially brought up by either you or counsel that was representing your client, is that correct? That is correct. And was it brought up more from your perspective, a positive thing or a negative thing to the trial judge?

speaker: matthewmclain
text: I think it was brought up to be a positive thing to us, or at least to make the court aware that, look, he has the potential of being deported and the court should be aware of that fact and that he does have plans for being deported if that were to happen. And he does have plans if he were to remain in the United States.

speaker: randwallis
text: And so that was the negative consequence for him personally that he could be deported, is that correct?

speaker: matthewmclain
text: Sure, yeah, that could be a negative.

speaker: randwallis
text: But we need to look at the overall, the impact or what is going to be the relationship going forward once he, if he was granted some type of release, because I believe the court was also having to consider what type of monitoring was going to take place if the court would be inclined to grant that release such as probation, is that correct? That is correct. So isn't it, shouldn't we be looking at that and looking at it from the perspective of the trial judge to see, okay, what options are gonna be available for control or checking in, community control, probation? It's improper for us to not allow the trial judge to consider all of the options with regard to that, is that correct?

speaker: matthewmclain
text: I think that's fair assessment, yes, your honor.

speaker: randwallis
text: Okay, so my understanding of the record on appeal that that was taken into account and specifically the judge was informed that if your client was released and was deported, there was going to be no control such as probation, community control or any type of monitoring with any certainty as the trial judge considered the release at that point, is that right?

speaker: matthewmclain
text: I don't know what the supervision would have been. I mean, if you're placed on probation, you still have reporting requirements and to the extent that he could still comply with those conditions in a different country, I think that certainly could still occur. Whether you can obviously arrest him for a violation of probation, that would be based off a willful substantial violation, that may be something that would be difficult to prove for the state, but I think if he's placed on probation, he's still on probation no matter where he's at.

speaker: randwallis
text: Well, was the trial judge given any clarity or any additional information as far as what options there would have been for that? Like if you say he's deported, I think it was Trinidad, is that correct? That's correct. Okay, so if he's deported and goes back to Trinidad, was the trial judge ever given any additional information by either party as far as how he would go about reporting for probation?

speaker: matthewmclain
text: No, your honor. Okay. And ultimately the problem in this case is not that it was just a consideration to be made by the court, but ultimately the court seems to have adopted a wholesale rule that if you are subject to deportation, that somehow prohibits you from getting a modification in the case. And that-

speaker: meredithsasso
text: I think, especially the way it was framed in the motion for modification, one of the, I guess the primary argument was that he would be under the watchful eye of specifically the Florida Department of Corrections. So why wasn't the court just addressing that argument that in fact he would not be under, and that's the way the court concluded the order. The result is that he would no longer, it would no longer be possible for him to be under the supervision of FDIC, therefore this court finds it should not be modified.

speaker: matthewmclain
text: And obviously that's not supported by the record because we don't know what's going to happen to him. He has a detainer, he'd go through the immigration process and there's a possibility that he does remain in the United States. So it's not fair for the court to say, well, because there's potential that you may be deported.

speaker: meredithsasso
text: Is that the standard though? I mean, the court is required to find fitness to reenter society and if the court does not have comfort that he is in fact fit to reenter society because he won't be under the watchful eye of it, because there is no assurance that he would be in fact under the watchful eye of FDIC, doesn't that kind of shift the trial court's burden?

speaker: matthewmclain
text: I don't think it does. And I don't think it has anything to do with his fitness to reenter society. That's something that he cannot prevent. He immigrated to this country legally at a young age. So if that's the situation, if we're gonna go ahead and look at, well, we can't guarantee somebody with an immigration detainer can be under the watchful eye of the Department of Corrections, that's a valid basis to deny modification of their sentence based off the principles established in Miller and Graham. Miller and Graham were set forth based off the principle of juveniles are capable of change and rehabilitation and they can reenter society. So if you think about in the most egregious circumstances, a defendant who is sentenced to life in prison and they have an immigration detainer, is a judge therefore allowed to deny sentence modification because they can't guarantee they'll remain in the United States? It seems to run counter to the principles of Graham and Miller in juvenile resentencing. We can't set forth that sort of precedent, especially when it has nothing to do with how can, in my opinion, a juvenile offender who has an immigration detainer can't do anything to prevent that from occurring. And it comes even in greater question in this case, because we don't know what's gonna happen to him in a situation with the deportation. I think you would know-

speaker: meredithsasso
text: Let me ask you about that. I mean, you noted that this did arise in the order. So although it was somewhat introduced by counsel below, but even in the brief, there's not a fundamental error argument. There's not a, as to point one, or as to point three, but there's not a specific due process or equal protection argument. In terms of our role in addressing issues raised by the party, what is the legal error that we're correcting and on what basis it's actually been argued in point one of the brief?

speaker: matthewmclain
text: I think point one was raised under abuse of discretion de novo and fundamental error. That was a standard review set forth in argument one and for all the arguments. And generally, a court's sentencing decision is reviewed for an abuse of discretion. So considering all these factors, did the court abuse discretion? I believe the argument was preserved by stating that it should not be viewed as a negative, but as an incentive for the court to go ahead and do modification. And as far as fundamental error, that argument was raised and impermissible sentencing factors do constitute fundamental error. When you look at the case, it's really disheartening because the court lists a number of factors, again, for his benefit and against him. And the judge never reaches a conclusion as to has he demonstrated rehabilitation? Is he fits Rancher Society? Instead, and this is where the problem really lies, the sole factor is he might be deported. And therefore, we're not gonna go ahead and modify his sentence.

speaker: meredithsasso
text: What if we disagree with that characterization and we frame it as the sole factor is that he would not be under the watchful eye of the Department of Corrections?

speaker: matthewmclain
text: I think that still presents a problem.

speaker: meredithsasso
text: Is that still impermissible?

speaker: matthewmclain
text: Yeah, absolutely it's impermissible because again, you would be setting a categorical rule that somebody who is subject to deportation cannot have their sentence modified because of the possibility that they get deported. That can't be the law, especially in light of the principles establishing Graham and Miller. The consequences would be too great and anybody who has a deportation hold, the judge can simply say, look, he might be deported, I don't know, but he might not be under the watchful eyes of the Department of Corrections. Therefore, I deny his sentence modification.

speaker: meredithsasso
text: It wouldn't be a categorical rule. I mean, you could conceive of an example where a judge might have no concern at all based on maybe the crime or maybe what the offender had demonstrated during their time incarceration, that the judge would not be worried about the possibility for probation and could release someone who might be deported.

speaker: matthewmclain
text: I think that's an excellent point, Your Honor. And that didn't happen in this case. There was no overall consideration. It just came down to, he might be deported, therefore, I'm gonna deny review. Had the judge taken a totality of a circumstances approach and said, look, I find that you are not rehabilitated, you are not fit to reenter society, and moreover, there's no guarantee you get under the watchful eye of supervision, then I'm going to deny you. So I think there's certain circumstances, you're right, where it could be a factor, but in this case-

speaker: meredithsasso
text: Didn't the trial court, though, indicate on the record that it had weighed both the statutory and non-statutory factors in reaching its decision?

speaker: matthewmclain
text: I think that it did in the final part, but you look at the court's order and it says the result of this is that it would no longer be possible for the defendants to be under the supervision of the Florida Department of Corrections. Therefore, this court finds the sentence should not be modified. And again, in the conclusion, it talks about immigration consequences and considering all the factors, but it never reached a conclusion, like Your Honor's suggesting, that he has not demonstrated rehabilitation, he's not fit. And even when you look at the court's findings as it relates to, does he pose a lesser risk to society, the court doesn't even answer that question. It lists facts, but it doesn't come to a conclusion. And that's ultimately the issue, there's findings of facts made by the court, but never a determination as to, this person is not rehabilitated, they do not pose a higher risk to society, nothing like that, it all comes down to immigration. And that's where we run into the problem of this sole issue of deportation becoming the problem and the cause for reversible error. I see I have two more minutes before my rebuttals, so I'd like to go ahead and address the third issue.

speaker: orfinger
text: I do have one other question for you. Yes, Your Honor. Why did you present, or why did the defendant present the fact that he was subject to the immigration order as an incentive to put him on probation? In what way would that be a positive?

speaker: matthewmclain
text: So the positive is that he has a 30 year sentence, he had done almost 25 years of his sentence at that point. He had no probation to follow. So the pitch to the court was, look, if he were to remain in the United States, let's put him on probation so we have some sort of supervision over him. Let's take this opportunity in the event, the possibility that he remains here to put him on supervision so we can have a watchful eye on him. Let's give him that benefit, let's give society that benefit. And if he's deported, he will still be on probation, likely it won't be enforceable, it'll be difficult to enforce, but we still account for the possibility that if he's detained by ICE and he's released in the US, that he should be on probation and not just released in society after the expiration of his non-probation sentence in the situation. Does that answer your question, Your Honor? It does. So regarding the third issue, that has to do with the court's use of subsequent misconducts in evaluating Mr. Sagar's defense and this decision to not modify his sentence. There's 28 disciplinary reports or 24 disciplinary reports in the case. The state was able to question Mr. Sagar about those disciplinary reports. He admitted to 18 of those disciplinary reports, but he specifically denied six of them. And one in particular, which the court found to be the most egregious was aggravated assault, aggravated battery on another prisoner. The problem with it that we have is that there's a case, Norville v. State, which talks about subsequent misconduct without conviction violates due process rights. There was no evidence presented by the state other than business records from the Florida Department of Corrections to support such an allegation. And when somebody specifically denies misconduct, there has to be some sort of reliable evidence that would go ahead and refute it for the court to be able to support a finding that a disciplinary report action did occur, but there was none. There's no conviction. There's no arrest. There's solely disciplinary report, which is denied. And interestingly, the records of the court relied upon as far as several of the incidents are specifically contradicted by other witness statements. So you have a disciplinary report that's denied. You have a disciplinary report that does not lead to an arrest or conviction. And you have a lot of evidence that demonstrates that the disciplinary report did not occur, yet you're holding that against the defendant. When a disciplinary report is not supported, although it could be relevant, if it's not supported, it should not be factored into the decision to not modify a sentence in the case. If there are no further questions, I'll reserve the remainder of my time.

speaker: randwallis
text: Okay, thank you, Mr. McClain. And we have Mr. Pallas. You may proceed when you are ready.

speaker: richardpallas
text: Thank you, Your Honor, and good morning. May it please the court, my name is Richard Pallas. I represent the state of Florida. Regarding the first issue of the deportation consequences, the state reasserts that that wasn't preserved through 38B or even a motion for clarification. But the state agrees with the way that the court has posited this issue, that it's not the fact that he's someone under an immigration status, it's that he's not going to finish this supervision. He won't be under the supervision if he is in fact deported.

speaker: meredithsasso
text: In fact- How do you respond to the argument that the only category of offenders that would not be subject to, or not have the potential to be supervised on probation are those that would be deported?

speaker: richardpallas
text: I don't believe that's necessarily what happened here, Your Honor. There's always the possibility that someone will say, I'm looking to leave the state. I have work in another state. I have work out of the country. I don't want to be here. I don't see why anyone would testify to such a thing when they're asking for release to be under supervision of the Florida Department of Corrections. But if the Florida Department of Corrections is not willing to transfer this supervision to another area, I believe that that falls in this same category, Your Honor. Now, again, this isn't anything like the supplemental authority that was recently filed by the defendant. In that case, it was sentencing, which is distinguishable from this because we're at a sentence review hearing instead to find out whether it should be modified. And moreover, the language used by the court that made that sentence subject to reversal is not at all what we have here. In fact, they were specifically stating members of the Asiatic community. They are specifically talking about people who are non-citizens in those two comments. Here, the judge, in its order, specifically talks about how the sentence memorandum or memorandum in favor of modification of probation stated he will be under the watchful eye of the Department of Corrections. However, the court then points out how this is running counterproductive to the fact he may not be under that watchful eye. And it would no longer be possible to supervise him if he is in fact taken out of this country. It would be nice if we had more evidence provided that of what his necessary fight on appeal would be, but none of that was presented by defendant. This is defendant's burden to prove that he is fit to reenter society. And if you can't prove you're going to get out and you're going to be on probation, then you're not fit to reenter society. We can't supervise him.

speaker: meredithsasso
text: And let's say that we agree that there's a distinction between sentencing and a review hearing. How does that play into your preservation analysis and that a 3800B motion was required?

speaker: richardpallas
text: Yes, Your Honor. Specifically with that, the state filed a supplemental authority recently that should have been included in its answer brief.

speaker: meredithsasso
text: Yes, and I reviewed that authority, but putting the case aside from a matter of course principles, how do you think that conforts with the plain language of the rule?

speaker: richardpallas
text: Well, the state acknowledges that both of our sides here are stating this case should not apply because it's a sentence review hearing and not sentencing itself. We're both saying that, and I understand how counterintuitive that seems, but here they had opportunities to move for rehearing, in my opinion, because the fact that this is leading to the next step, which is a sentencing, in this case, another resentencing for him, if he was agreed granted modification. I think that it just seems that the logical step would be to use the mechanisms for reviewing or correcting sentencing errors. But at least touching upon also the disciplinary reports, I don't see how this could be made precedent. This is one of our only snapshots of how he behaves in there. The state should not have to put him on trial for each and every indiscretion he had. Yes, he denied these. It's the trial court's discretion whether or not he's going to believe him. Now, we're not going to bring in every witness. The defendant could have brought in these witnesses. The trial court could have assessed their credibility in whether or not, oh, he did not participate in this riot or he did not commit this aggravated assault or battery. We have none of that on the record instead. All we have are his denials, which the court can choose to disregard. And even without these disciplinary reports, the court, in theory, regarding the second issue with its findings of whether he's rehabilitated and fit to reenter society, the court made negative findings in regarding to his participation in this crime. It made findings that the victims next of kin would prefer that he finishes his sentence. Well, one of them at the very least. I don't want to miscategorize the record, your honors. And the court then decided to additionally consider the fact that he's not going to be on supervision. And it's important to note, yes, the court says, therefore, sentence should not be modified after considering the fact that he may be deported. It seems to the state like it's very much going to happen that he's going to be deported or he's going to be in ICE custody. I'm not at all an expert on the appellate process when it comes to orders of deportation, but just knowing what I know of regular appellate procedure in the criminal context, I don't see how we're bringing in these additional facts. I mean, this was a random, senseless act of violence that this defendant helped plan. He did not actually commit the atrocity, but he helped cover it up. And he was there to help this happen in the first place. In the reply brief, the defendant states that the statement of deportation is one of the most egregious factors that could be considered. In the context of the defendant's supplemental authority of Lange, or Lange, I apologize for the mispronunciation, that would be one of the egregious moments where we're saying, you're a non-citizen. You're not a member of this country. And for that, I don't, in that case, it was for that reason, I want to give you this negative sentence. That's not what happened here. He stated, because the fact that you are being deported, you're not going to be under the watchful eye of the Department of Corrections as you asked us to put you under. And for that reason, I don't think you're fit to enter society, which leads me into point two, the court did not use those magic words. But also with the Dixon case, while those magic words were included in that order, the defendant was arguing, the court never said it considered the factors. That was expressly implied because the court listed those factors under section 921.1402. The court did not say in consideration of those factors, modification isn't appropriate, but it was clearly inferred. Here, the court said it considered these factors as well as his deportation consequences. But it then said, based on both of these, some modification should not happen at this time. The plain language of 1402 does not say the trial court must in its written order say you are unfit, that you are rehabilitated or you are not rehabilitated. It just states to issue a written order, stating the reasons why the sentence is not being modified. That language was applied in the Dixon case that the state supplemented with regarding that issue. It's very consistent with this one as well. And the fact is, we're not looking at whether or not he should get modification because he needs to be rehabilitated and fit to enter society. In the court, it's or. The language specifically states, he's not demonstrated rehabilitation or is unfit to enter society. Here, the fact that he may not be on supervision, that is perfectly on the other side of or, that he's unfit to reenter society because he will not be under supervision like the defendant stated he would be. If this court has no other questions, I will rely on my brief and I ask that you affirm the trial court's order denying modification of his sentence.

speaker: randwallis
text: Okay, thank you. Thank you. Mr. McLean, you got a little over three minutes.

speaker: matthewmclain
text: Thank you. And what makes this case so egregious is the fact that we don't know how the court ultimately judged Mr. Sagar. Again, going through the different factors, as opposing counsel points out, they made findings for and against Mr. Sagar. We don't know whether the court ultimately found he's demonstrated maturity and rehabilitation. All that we know based off this order is that regardless of any showing of rehabilitation, you might get deported. Therefore, we're denying your modification. There can be no other reading from the court's order. Unlike what your Honor said, Judge Zasso, there's no explanation of... We find that since you haven't demonstrated a ton of maturity and rehabilitation, sending you on to society with the possibility of not having supervision in a different country is something that we cannot allow.

speaker: meredithsasso
text: That wasn't... In terms of alienage though, the court did state on the record that if the court, it would be nice to have some assurances suggesting that if there was an assurance that there wouldn't be deportation, that the court might not have an issue with early release. And so doesn't that demonstrate that it wasn't necessarily the factor of alienage because the court was willing to release despite that factor. It was in fact the ability to be observed, basically.

speaker: matthewmclain
text: I don't think that's the situation. I think what happened was you can't predict a future event. And so how are you supposed to go and say, once he's detained by ICE and goes through the proper proceedings, he's gonna be deported? Basically, the court is asking for the defendant to be able to show that he is not gonna be deported or he is gonna be deported. And that can't be established. And it certainly presents interesting arguments to immigration that this is a juvenile offender who would be placed on probation in the United States. Why wouldn't he be able to stay? When his family's here, they legally migrated. We don't know what's gonna ultimately happen in that situation. It's unfair to have a litigant prove something that might happen in the future. It's an impossible burden.

speaker: orfinger
text: But there is an order from immigration ordering him deported as it stands now, correct?

speaker: matthewmclain
text: There was a detainer. I think the evidence introduces that there's a detainer. I don't recall whether there's an actual deportation order, but I imagine what would have happened is he would have been detained and then subject to deportation proceedings going forward. And he could contest those deportation proceedings as he sees fit. So as far as the order, that wasn't introduced into the record. I thought I heard it phrased that way. I had to check the record. I can't recall exactly the phrase, Your Honor, but my understanding is that there was a detainer. If there was a deportation order, again, that's something that can be contested and was being contested. And as far as preservation with a 1,300 B2, that's not a requirement. This is a sentence review proceeding. This is not a sentencing proceeding. Rule 3802 does not have a rehearing provision, nor does it reference 1,300 B2 as a requirement to preserve any sort of abuse of discretion or fundamental error argument. And finally, in regards to Dixon, Dixon says a 1,300 B2 motion should have been filed or motion of clarification, but ultimately the court still reviewed the issue for fundamental error. It did not find the issue to be waived. And thank you, Your Honor, so very much.

speaker: randwallis
text: Thank you, Mr. McLean and Mr. Kalas. And we are.
